custom-editors.html.summary: Custom node editors When the default node editor is not a good fit (e.g., you want hint texts, validation, or a layout tailored to the type) supply your own editor by deriving from NodeEditorBase<T>. WinForms Eto.Forms Default node editor PropertyGridNodeEditor<T> PropertyEditorNodeEditor<T> Base class for custom editors NodeEditorBase<T> (a UserControl) NodeEditorBase<T> (a Panel) Deriving from NodeEditorBase<T> NodeEditorBase<T> implements INodeEditor<T>. It exposes Bind() helpers that wire a control to a PropertyPointer<T> through the editor's undo system. You typically build the control hierarchy in the constructor. WinForms Eto.Forms public class AddressEditor : NodeEditorBase<Address> { public AddressEditor() { var textBoxStreet = new HintTextBox {HintText = "Street", Dock = DockStyle.Top, Multiline = true, Height = 40}; var textBoxCity = new HintTextBox {HintText = "City", Dock = DockStyle.Top}; var textBoxCountry = new HintTextBox {HintText = "Country", Dock = DockStyle.Top}; Bind(textBoxStreet, PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.Street)); Bind(textBoxCity, PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.City)); Bind(textBoxCountry, PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.Country)); // Reverse order for "Dock" Controls.Add(textBoxCountry); Controls.Add(textBoxCity); Controls.Add(textBoxStreet); } } The Bind() helpers return the control, so that you can place it directly in an Eto layout: public class AddressEditor : NodeEditorBase<Address> { public AddressEditor() { Content = new TableLayout { Spacing = new(8, 4), Rows = { new TableRow(new Label {Text = "Street"}, new TableCell(Bind(new TextArea {Height = 50}, PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.Street)), scaleWidth: true)), new TableRow(new Label {Text = "City"}, Bind(new TextBox(), PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.City))), new TableRow(new Label {Text = "Country"}, Bind(new TextBox(), PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => Target!.Country))), new TableRow {ScaleHeight = true} } }; } } Target! is safe to dereference inside the PropertyPointer lambda. The pointer is evaluated lazily after Target has been assigned by the host editor. Available Bind() overloads WinForms Eto.Forms Overload Use for Bind(Control, PropertyPointer<string?>) Any Control.Text-based input (TextBox, HintTextBox, ...) Bind(ComboBox, PropertyPointer<string?>) ComboBox, adds the current value to Items if missing Bind(UriTextBox, PropertyPointer<Uri?>) Uri properties, with validation Bind(CheckBox, PropertyPointer<bool>) bool properties Bind<TControl, TChild>(TControl, Func<TChild>) Nested INodeEditor<TChild> controls, propagates Target and CommandExecutor Overload Use for Bind<TControl>(TControl, PropertyPointer<string?>) Any TextControl (TextBox, TextArea, ...) Bind(ComboBox, PropertyPointer<string?>) Editable ComboBox Bind(UriTextBox, PropertyPointer<Uri?>) Uri properties, with validation Bind(CheckBox, PropertyPointer<bool>) bool properties Bind<TControl, TChild>(TControl, Func<TChild>) Nested INodeEditor<TChild> controls, propagates Target and CommandExecutor Text input is applied when the control loses focus, when Enter is pressed in a single-line control, and when CommitPendingChanges() is called. The structure editor calls this before the selection changes. Each binding writes through ICommandExecutor when present, so every change becomes an undoable command. If no executor is attached, the pointer is set directly. Plugging the editor in Pass an instance to the relevant fluent-API method instead of relying on the default node editor: editor.Describe<Contact>() .AddProperty("Home Address", x => PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => x.HomeAddress), new AddressEditor()) .AddProperty("Work Address", x => PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => x.WorkAddress), new AddressEditor()); The editor parameter is a dummy instance used solely for type inference of the generic editor type; the structure editor instantiates a fresh editor per node via new TEditor(). Refresh and lifecycle hooks NodeEditorBase<T> exposes protected events for advanced scenarios: TargetChanged: fires when a new Target is assigned. Use it to refresh control state that does not flow through Bind(). CommandExecutorChanged: fires when the undo system is (re)attached. OnRefresh: fires from Refresh(), both on target change and when external edits (e.g., the text editor) mutate the target. OnCommitPendingChanges (Eto.Forms only): fires from CommitPendingChanges(). Use it for controls that hold input of their own until they lose focus. The Bind() helpers subscribe to these internally, so you usually only need them when integrating controls that have no matching overload.

custom-frontends.html.title: Custom frontends | NanoByte Structure Editor
custom-frontends.html.summary: Custom frontends The library is split across multiple NuGet packages so the description model can be reused independently of the GUI toolkit. Two frontends are provided: WinForms and Eto.Forms. Both are built on the same toolkit-neutral core described below, which you can also use to build a frontend for another toolkit. The assemblies NanoByte.StructureEditor UI-agnostic. Defines: IStructureEditor<T>: the fluent entry point (DescribeRoot, Describe<TContainer>). IContainerDescription<TContainer> and IListDescription<TContainer, TList>: the fluent surface for declaring properties, plain lists, and polymorphic lists. Node and its concrete subclasses: runtime nodes returned by GetNodesIn(container), each carrying the methods needed to serialize, update, remove, and edit the underlying object. NodeCandidate: describes a node that could be created (drives "Add" menus), with GetCreateCommand() to materialize it. INodeEditor / INodeEditor<T>: the toolkit-neutral contract a per-type editor implements. StructureEditorPresenter<T>: the toolkit-neutral logic shared by all frontends (collecting descriptions, dispatching by container type, tracking the selection, add/remove and text round-tripping). The package targets net45 and net10.0. The non-Framework targets carry no Windows-specific dependencies, so it can be referenced from non-Windows hosts. NanoByte.StructureEditor.WinForms The frontend for Windows Forms (Windows). Provides: StructureEditor<T>: the UserControl that hosts the tree, per-node editor panel, and text editor (see Serialization formats). PropertyGridNodeEditor<T>: default INodeEditor<T> based on PropertyGrid. NodeEditorBase<T>: base class for custom editors, with Bind() helpers that wire WinForms controls to the undo system (see Custom editors). NanoByte.StructureEditor.EtoForms The frontend for Eto.Forms (Windows, Linux, macOS). Provides: StructureEditor<T>: the Panel that hosts the tree, per-node editor panel, and text editor. PropertyEditorNodeEditor<T>: default INodeEditor<T> based on PropertyEditor from NanoByte.Common.EtoForms. NodeEditorBase<T>: base class for custom editors, with Bind() helpers that wire Eto controls to the undo system (see Custom editors). ITextEditor: abstraction for the text pane. The default PlainTextEditor is a monospaced TextArea; set TextEditorFactory.Default during application startup, before creating any structure editors, to plug in an editor with syntax highlighting. Runtime flow Description: your code calls DescribeRoot() / Describe<TContainer>() and the fluent methods, populating a per-container-type list of node descriptions. Dispatch: StructureEditorPresenter<T> stores these descriptions in an AggregateDispatcher keyed by container type. To build the tree, the frontend walks the object graph and the presenter dispatches each object to the matching description list. Node materialization: each description yields concrete Node instances. The frontend wraps them in tree items of its toolkit. Editing: selecting a tree node calls Node.GetEditorControl(executor), which returns an INodeEditor bound to the current CommandManager. Changes flow as IUndoCommands onto the shared undo stack. Serialization: the text editor mirrors Node.GetSerialized(serializer) for the selected node, using an IStructureSerializer such as XmlStructureSerializer. Edits there round-trip via Node.GetUpdateCommand(serializedValue, serializer), which replaces the target with the deserialized value as an undoable command. Building another frontend Because IStructureEditor<T>, Node, and INodeEditor are toolkit-neutral, a host for Avalonia, WPF, Uno, etc. can be built without touching the core package. The WinForms and Eto.Forms frontends are good references. A minimal port needs to: Implement IStructureEditor<T> by delegating to a StructureEditorPresenter<T>. Call its Close() method when your control is disposed. Render the node tree by walking GetRootNodes() and GetNodes(node.Target) recursively. Report the selected node via Select(). Rebuild the tree after calling Open() and whenever StructureChanged is raised, using ShouldSelect() to restore the selection. Provide a toolkit-specific INodeEditor<T> base class (analogous to NodeEditorBase<T>) that adapts your toolkit's data-binding to PropertyPointer<T> and ICommandExecutor. Populate "Add" menus from GetCandidates() and pass the chosen one to Add(). null entries mark where to place separators. The text editor pane is optional. To provide one, show GetSerialized() for the selected node and pass edited text to UpdateFromText(). The rest of the model works the same whether or not you expose the serialized form.

index.html.title: Home | NanoByte Structure Editor
index.html.summary: NanoByte Structure Editor NanoByte Structure Editor is a .NET library that helps you build split-screen editors for your data structures, consisting of: a collapsible tree-view of the data structure, a graphical editor for the currently selected node in the tree (auto-generated or custom) and a text editor with a serialized (XML or JSON) representation of the currently selected node. This allows you to create an IDE-like experience for your users when editing complex domain specific languages, configuration files, etc.. Choosing a frontend The library is available for two GUI toolkits. Both share the same API for describing your data structure, storage and undo/redo. Add a reference to the NuGet package matching your application: NanoByte.StructureEditor.WinForms NanoByte.StructureEditor.EtoForms GUI toolkit Windows Forms Eto.Forms Platforms Windows Windows, Linux, macOS Frameworks .NET Framework 4.5+, .NET 10.0+ .NET Framework 4.7.2+, .NET 10.0+ Editor control StructureEditor<T> StructureEditor<T> Default node editor PropertyGridNodeEditor<T> PropertyEditorNodeEditor<T> Text editor ICSharpCode.TextEditor with syntax highlighting Plain monospaced text box, replaceable via TextEditorFactory.Default Sample Sample.WinForms Sample.EtoForms An Eto.Forms application additionally needs an Eto.Platform.* package for each platform it runs on (e.g., Eto.Platform.Windows, Eto.Platform.Gtk, Eto.Platform.Mac64). Code snippets in this documentation work with both packages unless shown in separate tabs or marked otherwise. Import the namespace matching your package (NanoByte.StructureEditor.WinForms or NanoByte.StructureEditor.EtoForms). Usage Initialization Create an instance of StructureEditor<T> and add it to your Form: WinForms Eto.Forms var editor = new StructureEditor<MyData>(); Controls.Add(editor); var editor = new StructureEditor<MyData>(); form.Content = editor; Alternatively, you may want to derive your own class from StructureEditor<T>. This lets you keep the description of your data structure in one place and, with WinForms, use the graphical designer in Visual Studio (which does not support generic types) to place the editor on your Form. public class MyDataEditor : StructureEditor<MyData> {} You need to "describe" your data structure to the editor. You can do this directly after instantiating the editor or in the constructor of your derived class. Call DescribeRoot() and then use the fluent API provided as a return value to describe the properties on your main data type. Call Describe () to describe the properties on a data type TContainer exposed by another property. You can use multiple calls with different type parameters to describe arbitrarily deep hierarchies. The fluent API provides the following methods: .AddProperty() describes a property. .AddRequiredProperty() describes a property that cannot be set to null. .AddPolymorphicProperty() describes a polymorphic property. After calling it you chain .AddElement() calls for each specific type the property can hold. .AddRequiredPolymorphicProperty() describes a polymorphic property that cannot be set to null. .AddList() describes a list. .AddPolymorphicList() describes a polymorphic list. After calling it you need to chain .AddElement() calls for each specific type of element the list can hold. There are numerous overloads for each of these methods, e.g., allowing you to specify a custom editor control for a data type or to keep the auto-generated one. editor.DescribeRoot("Address Book") .AddList("Group", x => x.Groups); editor.Describe<IContactContainer>() .AddList("Contact", x => x.Contacts); editor.Describe<Contact>() .AddRequiredProperty("Home Address", x => PropertyPointer.For(() => x.HomeAddress)) .AddProperty("Work Address", x => PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => x.WorkAddress)) .AddPolymorphicList(x => x.PhoneNumbers) .AddElement("Landline Number", () => new LandlineNumber()) .AddElement("Mobile Number", () => new MobileNumber()); Storage Use the Open() method to load an XML file into the editor: editor.Open(CommandManager<AddressBook>.Load(path)); Use the Save() method on the CommandManager property to save the editor's content as an XML file: editor.CommitPendingChanges(); // Eto.Forms only editor.CommandManager.Save(path); With Eto.Forms, input in a control that still has the focus may not have been applied yet. Call CommitPendingChanges() before saving to make sure the latest input is included. See Undo, redo and persistence for details. Serialization formats The text editor uses XML by default. To use JSON (System.Text.Json) instead, add a reference to the NanoByte.StructureEditor.Json NuGet package and set the Serializer property to JsonStructureSerializer: editor.Serializer = JsonStructureSerializer.Instance; To load and save files in the same format, use SerializingCommandManager<T>. Passing one to Open() also sets the editor's Serializer: editor.Open(SerializingCommandManager<AddressBook>.Load(path, JsonStructureSerializer.Instance)); editor.CommandManager.Save(path); For Newtonsoft.Json, add a reference to the NanoByte.StructureEditor.NewtonsoftJson instead and use NewtonsoftJsonStructureSerializer. Polymorphic lists and properties need extra attributes or settings to round-trip through JSON. See Serialization formats for details. Samples Take a look at the sample projects for a more complete setup, including custom node editors and undo/redo functionality. Both use the same data model from Sample: Sample.WinForms Sample.EtoForms

polymorphic-lists.html.title: Polymorphic lists | NanoByte Structure Editor
polymorphic-lists.html.summary: Polymorphic lists AddList() covers the common case of a list with a single element type. When a list can hold multiple concrete types behind a common base class or interface, use AddPolymorphicList() and chain AddElement() for each concrete type the user should be able to add. Modeling the data The XML serializer needs to know which CLR types each list can contain. Annotate the list property with one [XmlElement] per concrete type, mapping the element name to the type: public abstract class PhoneNumber { public string? CountryCode { get; set; } public string? AreaCode { get; set; } public string? LocalNumber { get; set; } } public class LandlineNumber : PhoneNumber { /* ... */ } public class MobileNumber : PhoneNumber { /* ... */ } public class Contact { [XmlElement(nameof(LandlineNumber), typeof(LandlineNumber))] [XmlElement(nameof(MobileNumber), typeof(MobileNumber))] public List<PhoneNumber> PhoneNumbers { get; } = []; } The element name passed to [XmlElement] is the XML tag that will appear in the serialized output and inside the embedded text editor. It does not have to match the CLR type name, but doing so keeps things obvious. When using JSON instead of XML, polymorphic types need a type discriminator instead. See Serialization formats. Describing the list AddPolymorphicList() returns an IListDescription<TContainer, TList> on which you call AddElement() once per concrete type. The user-facing name and factory you pass here populate the "Add" drop-down menu: editor.Describe<Contact>() .AddPolymorphicList(x => x.PhoneNumbers) .AddElement("Landline Number", () => new LandlineNumber()) .AddElement("Mobile Number", () => new MobileNumber()); Each AddElement() overload accepts an optional editor instance, the same way AddProperty() does. Pass a custom INodeEditor<T> if the default node editor is not enough: .AddElement("Landline Number", () => new LandlineNumber(), new LandlineEditor()) .AddElement("Mobile Number", () => new MobileNumber(), new MobileEditor()); Containers shared across multiple parents If several types expose the same kind of child collection, factor it out into an interface and call Describe<TInterface>(). The structure editor dispatches by runtime type, so any object implementing the interface picks up the description: public interface IContactContainer { List<Contact> Contacts { get; } } public class AddressBook : IContactContainer { /* ... */ } public class Group : IContactContainer { /* ... */ } editor.Describe<IContactContainer>() .AddList("Contact", x => x.Contacts); Both AddressBook nodes and Group nodes will now offer "Add → Contact" in the tree, without having to repeat the description.

polymorphic-properties.html.title: Polymorphic properties | NanoByte Structure Editor
polymorphic-properties.html.summary: Polymorphic properties AddProperty() covers the common case of a single-value property with a fixed type. When a property can hold one of several concrete types behind a common base class or interface, use AddPolymorphicProperty() and chain AddElement() for each concrete type the user should be able to set. Modeling the data The XML serializer needs to know which CLR types the property can hold. Annotate the property with one [XmlElement] per concrete type, mapping the element name to the type: public abstract class PhoneNumber { public string? CountryCode { get; set; } public string? AreaCode { get; set; } public string? LocalNumber { get; set; } } public class LandlineNumber : PhoneNumber { /* ... */ } public class MobileNumber : PhoneNumber { /* ... */ } public class Contact { [XmlElement(nameof(LandlineNumber), typeof(LandlineNumber))] [XmlElement(nameof(MobileNumber), typeof(MobileNumber))] public PhoneNumber? PrimaryNumber { get; set; } } The element name passed to [XmlElement] is the XML tag that will appear in the serialized output and inside the embedded text editor. It does not have to match the CLR type name, but doing so keeps things obvious. When using JSON instead of XML, polymorphic types need a type discriminator instead. See Serialization formats. Describing the property AddPolymorphicProperty() returns an IPropertyDescription<TContainer, TProperty> on which you call AddElement() once per concrete type. The user-facing name and factory you pass here populate the "Add" drop-down menu: editor.Describe<Contact>() .AddPolymorphicProperty(x => PropertyPointer.ForNullable(() => x.PrimaryNumber)) .AddElement("Primary Landline Number", () => new LandlineNumber()) .AddElement("Primary Mobile Number", () => new MobileNumber()); Because the property holds at most one value, the editor offers the configured types in the "Add" menu only while the property is unset, and setting one replaces any previous value. Each AddElement() overload accepts an optional editor instance, the same way AddProperty() does. Pass a custom INodeEditor<T> if the default node editor is not enough: .AddElement("Primary Landline Number", () => new LandlineNumber(), new LandlineEditor()) .AddElement("Primary Mobile Number", () => new MobileNumber(), new MobileEditor());

serialization-formats.html.title: Serialization formats | NanoByte Structure Editor
serialization-formats.html.summary: Serialization formats The text editor shows a serialized representation of the selected node. By default this is XML, but you can switch to JSON or plug in your own format. Serializer Package Frameworks XmlStructureSerializer (default) NanoByte.StructureEditor .NET Framework 4.5+, .NET 10.0+ JsonStructureSerializer (System.Text.Json) NanoByte.StructureEditor.Json .NET Framework 4.7.2+, .NET 10.0+ NewtonsoftJsonStructureSerializer (Newtonsoft.Json) NanoByte.StructureEditor.NewtonsoftJson .NET Framework 4.5+, .NET 10.0+ Choosing a serializer Set the Serializer property of StructureEditor<T> or StructureEditor<T> to change the format of the text editor: editor.Serializer = JsonStructureSerializer.Instance; To load and save files in the same format, use SerializingCommandManager<T> instead of CommandManager<T> (which always uses XML). Passing one to Open() also sets the editor's Serializer: editor.Open(SerializingCommandManager<AddressBook>.Load(path, JsonStructureSerializer.Instance)); // ... editor.CommandManager.Save(path); Both JSON serializers accept options/settings in their constructors. Start from JsonStructureSerializer.DefaultOptions or NewtonsoftJsonStructureSerializer.DefaultSettings and adjust as needed. Modeling the data for JSON XML serialization attributes such as [XmlAttribute], [XmlElement] and [XmlIgnore] have no effect on JSON. Use the JSON library's own attributes (e.g., [JsonIgnore], [JsonPropertyName]) where needed. Get-only collections Lists exposed as get-only properties, such as public List<Contact> Contacts { get; } = [];, need to be populated in place rather than replaced: JsonStructureSerializer.DefaultOptions sets PreferredObjectCreationHandling = JsonObjectCreationHandling.Populate for this. Keep it if you provide your own options. Newtonsoft.Json populates existing collections by default. Polymorphism Polymorphic lists and polymorphic properties need a type discriminator in JSON, so the deserializer knows which concrete type to create. System.Text.Json: annotate the base type with [JsonPolymorphic] and one [JsonDerivedType] per concrete type: [JsonPolymorphic] [JsonDerivedType(typeof(LandlineNumber), nameof(LandlineNumber))] [JsonDerivedType(typeof(MobileNumber), nameof(MobileNumber))] public abstract class PhoneNumber { /* ... */ } The discriminator is written as a $type property. By default, it must be the first property of the object. On .NET 9+ you can set AllowOutOfOrderMetadataProperties = true to relax this. Newtonsoft.Json: enable TypeNameHandling.Auto. Always combine it with a SerializationBinder that only allows your own types. Otherwise, loading untrusted JSON can instantiate arbitrary types. editor.Serializer = new NewtonsoftJsonStructureSerializer(new JsonSerializerSettings { Formatting = Formatting.Indented, TypeNameHandling = TypeNameHandling.Auto, SerializationBinder = new KnownTypesBinder(typeof(LandlineNumber), typeof(MobileNumber)) }); class KnownTypesBinder(params Type[] knownTypes) : ISerializationBinder { public Type BindToType(string? assemblyName, string typeName) => knownTypes.FirstOrDefault(x => x.Name == typeName) ?? throw new JsonSerializationException($"Unknown type: {typeName}"); public void BindToName(Type serializedType, out string? assemblyName, out string? typeName) { assemblyName = null; typeName = serializedType.Name; } } When you select a single list element or property value in the tree, the text editor serializes it as its concrete type. So the discriminator only appears when you view the containing object. Custom formats Implement IStructureSerializer to support other formats (e.g., YAML): FormatName names the format (e.g., XML, JSON). The WinForms text editor uses it to select syntax highlighting; on Eto.Forms it is passed on to the ITextEditor. Serialize() and Deserialize() convert between objects and text. Deserialize() should throw on invalid input. TryGetErrorLocation() extracts a line and column from exceptions thrown by Deserialize(). The text editor uses this to underline the error.

undo-redo.html.title: Undo, redo and persistence | NanoByte Structure Editor
undo-redo.html.summary: Undo, redo and persistence The structure editor routes every edit (tree changes, property changes, and raw text edits) through a single ICommandManager<T>. The manager owns the root object, records reversible commands, and persists to disk. The CommandManager property StructureEditor<T>.CommandManager is the seam between the editor and your data. It is created automatically (wrapping a new T from the factory) and replaced when you call Open(): editor.Open(CommandManager<AddressBook>.Load(path)); // load from XML editor.Open(CommandManager.For(SampleData.AddressBook)); // wrap an in-memory object CommandManager.Target is the live root object. Reads and writes are safe at any time. Replacing it raises TargetUpdated, which the editor uses to rebuild the tree asynchronously. Saving CommandManager<T> serializes the target to XML. Use SerializingCommandManager<T> to save in another format, such as JSON (see Serialization formats): editor.CommandManager.Save(path); After Save(), CommandManager.UndoEnabled becomes false and Path is updated, so you can build a "dirty" indicator and a Save/Save As flow: public bool Save() { CommitPendingChanges(); // Eto.Forms only if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(CommandManager.Path)) return SaveAs(); CommandManager.Save(CommandManager.Path); return true; } With Eto.Forms, input in a control that still has the focus may not have been applied yet. Call CommitPendingChanges() before reading or saving CommandManager.Target to make sure the latest input is included. Wiring undo/redo into your UI StructureEditor<T> exposes Undo() and Redo() methods. They delegate to CommandManager.Undo() / Redo(), reversing the last structural or property change. WinForms Eto.Forms If the embedded text editor has its own undo stack populated (i.e., the user is typing), Undo() and Redo() undo/redo characters there instead. Bind them to menu items or hot-keys: new ToolStripMenuItem("&Undo") {ShortcutKeys = Keys.Control | Keys.Z} .Click += (_, _) => editor.Undo(); Undo() and Redo() first apply any pending input, so that it can be undone as well. Bind them to menu items or hot-keys: var item = new ButtonMenuItem {Text = "&Undo", Shortcut = Application.Instance.CommonModifier | Keys.Z}; item.Click += (_, _) => editor.Undo(); Confirming unsaved changes on close Check CommandManager.UndoEnabled to detect pending changes: public bool Closing() { CommitPendingChanges(); // Eto.Forms only if (!CommandManager.UndoEnabled) return true; return Msg.YesNoCancel(this, "Save changes?", MsgSeverity.Warn) switch { DialogResult.Yes => Save(), DialogResult.No => true, _ => false }; } Custom editors and the command system Inside a NodeEditorBase<T> (NodeEditorBase<T> or NodeEditorBase<T>), the Bind() helpers route changes through ICommandExecutor (CommandExecutor), which is the same instance as the structure editor's CommandManager. You generally do not need to interact with it directly. If you build a control without a matching Bind() overload, pass the new value to the protected SetValue() helper: SetValue(pointer, newValue); It executes a SetValueCommand on the CommandExecutor. If no executor is attached, it sets the pointer directly. This is equivalent to: if (CommandExecutor == null) pointer.Value = newValue; else CommandExecutor.Execute(SetValueCommand.For(pointer, newValue)); Use this longer form if you need to execute a different kind of command. This keeps property edits, tree add/remove, and raw text edits on one undo stack, so a single Ctrl+Z reverses whichever happened last.
